name: Inbound iMessage attachments (photos, PDFs, voice memos)
description: Photos, PDFs and voice memos sent to Happy actually reach the agent; today a message that is only an attachment is dropped without a reply.
how: Set channels.imessage.includeAttachments: true; Basic mode already carries media; default attachment root covers the happy user; inbound caps are 10 MB image, 20 MB audio.
corrections: Catalog JSON 'needs' asks for an attachmentRoots entry and treats mediaMaxMb 16 as the limit for incoming files. media.md:23-25 says the default root pattern already covers every user's Messages folder (configured roots are merged, not replaced) and mediaMaxMb is the outbound cap. The Markdown wording already reflects this.

'Under store:false' covers less than it reads. OpenAI's data-controls page says store only governs application state; abuse-monitoring logs with prompt and response content are still kept up to 30 days by default. Family photos sent to the model fall under that unless the OpenAI organisation has Zero Data Retention.
unverified: That the gateway process under the happy account already has Full Disk Access to the Messages attachments folder comes from the 9 Oct notes and was not re-checked.
Whether OpenClaw treats the per-person custom provider ids exactly like the stock OpenAI provider for image input was not tested live (the config repo does declare image input for both models).

The minimal profile contains only session_status and gateway (tool-policy.md:36), and pdfModel is an agents.defaults key that is unset by default (pdf.md:124). The Markdown already drops both.

name: Voice memos in, transcribed locally
description: A parent sends a voice memo instead of typing; the Mac mini transcribes it locally, echoes the text back and answers. Only the transcript reaches the cloud model.
how: Explicit tools.media.models CLI entry (whisper-cli, capabilities audio, {{AttachmentPath}}) plus echoTranscript; needs brew whisper.cpp, ffmpeg and a GGML model file; OpenClaw converts to WAV itself.
corrections: Markdown pairs a whisper-cpp install with audio.preferredModel: "cli:whisper". The matcher compares that value with cli: plus the entry's exact command string (dist/resolve-KJuMET3H.mjs:148), so for whisper-cpp it must be cli:whisper-cli, or cli: plus the full path used in the entry; cli:whisper only matches the Python whisper CLI.

The Homebrew formula is now named whisper.cpp (formerly whisper-cpp) and its page says GGML model files are not downloaded by default. The 9 Oct note about a model that downloads automatically describes the Python whisper CLI (media-understanding.md:168), not whisper-cli.

ffmpeg is a hard requirement the Markdown leaves out: upstream whisper-cli reads only 16-bit WAV (github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp README), OpenClaw shells out to ffmpeg for that conversion (dist/ffmpeg-exec-VIr-PIWC.mjs:25 prints the brew install hint), and the formula does not pull ffmpeg in.
unverified: The container format of iMessage voice memos, and whether ffmpeg decodes it cleanly, were not tested.
Transcription speed on the M5 Pro and accuracy for Chinese or mixed-language speech were not measured.
Whether the per-person custom provider ids count as OpenAI audio auth in auto-detection is undocumented; the explicit CLI entry sidesteps the question.

name: Local neural voice for spoken replies (local-only once cloud speech is switched off)
description: Replaces the robotic macOS `say` voice from F004 with a natural voice synthesized entirely on the Mac mini, so read-aloud answers, briefs and later any kids' content never touch a cloud TTS provider. This is the piece every other voice feature borrows its speech from.
example: Parent texts: read me today's brief. Or sends `/tts latest` after a long answer and gets an audio file back in iMessage.
how: Gateway `tts` block. Documented option A: Speech Swift's local server on loopback (`brew install speech`, `speech-server --port 8080`) with the `openai` speech provider pointed at the loopback base URL, `model` tts-1 (which selects Kokoro) and `responseFormat` wav. Option B: `tts-local-cli` running the `speech` or `say` command. Option C: a Piper voice through sherpa-onnx; the bundled sherpa-onnx-tts skill runs a local binary from a shell, which needs an exec tool no agent here has, so in practice point `tts-local-cli` at that binary. In every option set `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled: false`, so the default-on Microsoft online provider cannot serve as a fallback when the local engine fails. Per-agent control through `agents.entries.<id>.tts` (off for research and inbox). `tts.auto: inbound` gives a voice answer to a voice memo; `/tts latest` reads the previous reply. ffmpeg on the host for conversions.
depends_on: Homebrew installs done from the admin account (speech, ffmpeg)
caveats: iMessage is not a voice-note channel: the reply is an audio file attachment, not a voice bubble. The voice-bubble option (`asVoice` on upload-file) belongs to the Private API action set, which needs SIP off.
Local engines emit WAV, so a few minutes of speech is several megabytes.
Long replies are summarized by the chat model before synthesis (a cloud call) or truncated.
Two tempting shortcuts are cloud services and must stay off for kids' content: the no-key Microsoft provider (Edge online TTS) and the bundled `sag` skill (ElevenLabs).
The built-in `tts` tool only speaks when asked, which is the right default: nobody wants every text reply doubled as audio.

Local-only is not the default. The keyless Microsoft provider is enabled by default, and the docs say other configured providers act as fallbacks, so a stopped local server could end in a cloud call unless Microsoft is disabled.

`/tts provider <id>` is open to any authorized sender and writes one preference file on the gateway host, so a single text can move speech to another provider for everyone. Having no cloud provider configured is the control; a prompt rule is not.

Option A adds a third-party Homebrew package and a long-running loopback server under the happy user, plus a model download: an install, a launch agent, a firewall rule and a one-time egress exception.
The loopback route needs Speech Swift v0.0.23 or later. It is a 0.0.x project, so pin the version and expect rough edges; the server also needs its own launchd job to stay up.
None of `speech`, `speech-server` or `ffmpeg` is installed on this Mac today.
iMessage outbound media is capped by `channels.imessage.mediaMaxMb` (default 16 MB), which bounds the length of a WAV reply.
safety: Speech synthesis is an output transformation on the gateway host and adds no new way for an agent to send data out. It is local-only, and so usable for kids' content later, only after the cloud speech providers are disabled in config and blocked at the proxy; the default provider chain and the provider slash command would otherwise allow a cloud voice. Long replies pass through a summary model before synthesis, which must be local or off for kids. Keep provider switching by directive off (VOX-03).
unverified: Kokoro or Piper voice quality and speed on this Mac.
Whether pointing `tts.providers.openai` at loopback has any side effect on the earlier decision not to add a catalog openai model provider (it is a different config block).
Whether scheduled announce deliveries (briefs) pass through Auto-TTS or only interactive replies do.
Whether the fallback chain actually reaches the Microsoft online voice when the selected local provider errors.
Which hosts the Speech Swift package contacts to download its models.

Whether a failed local synthesis actually falls through to the Microsoft online provider when only one provider block is written. The docs say other configured providers are fallbacks and that Microsoft is enabled by default; this was not tested.

One safety gap: the keyless Microsoft speech provider is an online service that is enabled by default, and configured providers act as fallbacks, so the promise that no text leaves the Mac only holds once `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled` is false. The sherpa-onnx option also needs rewording, since running it as a skill needs an exec tool no agent has.

name: In the car: Siri plus iMessage, with a driving reply style
description: While driving, a parent talks to Happy through what the car already has: Siri sends the iMessage and announces Happy's reply. Happy's part is a driving style: at most two short sentences, no links, no lists, numbers written for speech, details deferred until parked.
example: Hey Siri, text Happy: driving, what time does practice end and who has pickup?
how:
No new tool or plugin. A rule in each

-main AGENTS.md: when a message starts with the word driving (or the person says they are in the car), answer in at most two plain sentences and offer to send the rest later. Siri's message announcements in CarPlay do the listening and speaking.
caveats: I found no CarPlay surface in the installed OpenClaw docs or changelog (a search for the word returned nothing), so there is no Happy app on the car screen to plan for.
The OpenClaw Start Live Voice shortcut is not a car feature: it needs the phone unlocked and the app in the foreground.
Anything that needs a tap, such as an approval prompt, has to wait until parked.
This is mostly the phone doing its job; the only work is making Happy's replies fit to be read aloud.
Apple's page says that for long messages Siri announces only the sender and reads the text on request, which is the practical reason to keep replies to two sentences.
Announced replies are heard by everyone in the car, so the driving style should also hold back private detail (money, health, the other adult's plans) until parked.
The example needs calendar knowledge Happy does not have yet; today the rule only improves weather and search answers.

Apple's CarPlay page says that when a message is long, Siri announces only the sender's name and that a message arrived, and reads it in full only when asked. A long reply from Happy is therefore not heard unless the driver asks, which is the real reason for the two-sentence cap.
safety: Identical to typed iMessage: allowlisted sender, same agent, same hooks, same family-only outbound pin. No new device credential and no audio leaves the phone other than through Apple's own Siri.
unverified: How Siri handles long or multi-part replies in CarPlay.
Whether a voice memo (F003) can be recorded hands-free in CarPlay.
Apple's detailed CarPlay Messages pages returned only navigation when fetched, so only the general CarPlay support page is cited.
How long a message has to be before Siri stops reading it out, and how several messages in a row are announced.

A `before_dispatch` keyword hook that keeps a short-lived car flag on the session. The installed docs describe that hook as a claim on the inbound message, not a way to shape the reply, so the AGENTS.md rule is the mechanism to rely on.

name: Family delivery primitive: message an allowlisted family member or the group chat, recipient-pinned
description: Happy can pass a short text from one parent to the other or to the parents' group, and can never message anyone outside the family.
how:
message tool on

-main with a before_tool_call plugin hook that blocks any target not in family.json5 (fails closed); host jobs use openclaw agent --deliver or openclaw message send.
corrections: Markdown adds message_sending 'as a second gate'. That hook can cancel a send, but when its handler throws or times out it is logged and skipped (hooks/reference.md:94), so it fails open; only the before_tool_call check is fail-closed.

The 9 Oct 'needs' implies that enabling the tool plus the hook is enough. The live config turns both crossContext switches off, and tool-permissions.md:39 says that confines sends to the current conversation, so the same-provider switch must be re-opened and the hook then becomes the only recipient limit.
unverified: The exact parameter that carries the recipient in a message tool call, which the hook must match, was not read from source.
openclaw message send takes no agent flag and runs as the configured System Agent (cli/message.md:35-50); whether that suits per-person jobs was not tested.
The hook plugin and its family-only test case do not exist yet, so blocking an unknown recipient is unproven on this install.

name: Built-in chat commands for parents (/stop, /new, /btw, /status, /usage, /tools, /loop)
description: A handful of typed commands that already work in the iMessage thread: stop an answer that is going wrong, start a clean conversation, see what Happy can do right now, and check health and cost, all handled before any model call. Two more do use the model: /btw asks a side question that is not remembered, and /loop (owner only, once the scheduling tool is granted) starts a repeating check inside a thread.
example: Jordan texts '/stop' when a long answer is heading the wrong way, then '/new'. Tony texts '/loop 30m tell me when the winter storm warning ends'.
how:
Text commands are core and work on iMessage: command-only messages from allowlisted senders are handled before the queue and the model. /stop aborts the active run in that chat; /new archives the session and starts fresh; /tools lists the agent's effective tools; /status shows runtime, uptime and plugin health; /usage tokens|full|cost toggles a per-reply footer or prints a cost summary. /btw answers from the current session with a separate one-shot model query and writes nothing to history. /loop is owner-only and asks the agent to create a recurring agent-turn job bound to the conversation through the cron (automations) tool, at a fixed interval or self-paced between one minute and one hour, so it works only after F007 grants that tool to

-main. Put the five everyday ones in templates/person/AGENTS.md and a one-screen cheat sheet. The config-writing commands stay off as today, and Tony should decide whether /restart, which is on by default for owners, stays available from chat.
depends_on: F007 if Jordan should be able to use /loop (owner list)
G005 kill switch for the stop-everything case

F007 (automations/cron tool on

-main) before /loop works at all; Jordan in the owner list if she should use it
caveats: /stop ends one run in one chat; it does not pause scheduled jobs, so it complements the G005 kill phrase rather than replacing it.

/loop needs owner status, which only Tony has today, and it asks the agent to create the job with the cron (automations) tool, so it does nothing until

-main holds that tool (F007).
The /btw page names WhatsApp, Telegram and Discord for channel use and does not mention iMessage.
/usage figures are local estimates, like G004.
In a plain iMessage bubble the /status and /tools output may be long.

A /loop job is written by the model in chat, outside the G003 jobs registry, and is capped to the tools of the turn that created it; a self-paced loop may run as often as once a minute, so count it under G004 and review it with /loop status.
/btw is a separate one-shot model call on the session's model; it is not free and not model-less.
safety:
No new capability for the five everyday commands: they are read from the sender's own message, authorised by the sender allowlist and the owner list, and handled before the model runs. /btw and /loop are model turns on

-main under its normal tool policy, and

-main cannot browse. /loop additionally needs the cron tool and creates a job outside the registry, visible in the automations list (G003, G020); the job cannot hold more tools than the turn that created it.
unverified: Whether /btw works over the iMessage channel in 2026.9.7
How /status and /tools render in iMessage

name: Video clips sent to Happy
description: Parents will send short videos as naturally as photos: the dishwasher's blinking error, a recital clip, a how-to from the coach. On this provider set Happy cannot watch them. The bundled video-understanding providers are Google, Qwen and Moonshot, and none is configured. A local wrapper can at least transcribe the sound track.
example: Tony sends a 20-second clip of the furnace panel: 'What is it trying to tell me?'
how: Turning on channels.imessage.includeAttachments (F001) forwards video along with photos and voice memos. Media understanding then looks for a video-capable entry: the bundled order for video is Google, then Qwen, then Moonshot, with a 50 MB default input cap, and OpenAI is not in that list. Without such an entry the reply flow continues and the docs say the original media is still passed to the model; whether gpt-6-sol accepts a video file that way is untested. Honest options: (1) a line in AGENTS.md telling the sender to send a photo or a few screenshots instead; (2) a local CLI entry in tools.media.models with the video capability that runs an in-house script, in which ffmpeg extracts the audio track for the same local whisper path as voice memos (F003); (3) a Google key for video, which is a new vendor outside the store:false arrangement and is not proposed.
caveats: A still photo answers most of these questions and already works with photo understanding (F002).
Family videos contain the children's faces and voices. Any frames sent as images go to the cloud model under the same decision as photos (9 Oct decision 3).
iPhone clips are large; anything over the cap is skipped.
The docs' own command-line example for video calls a Gemini tool, which is the cloud route under another name.
The furnace-panel example is not served by the sound-track route: a silent clip of blinking lights yields an empty transcript. For that case the only working answer is 'send a photo'.
The video capability's default output limit is 500 characters, so a transcript route must raise maxChars on its entry or longer clips are cut short.
The family's provider entries declare text and image as model inputs (read-only check of the config repo), so video is not a declared input for either model today.
Neither ffmpeg nor a whisper binary was found under /opt/homebrew/bin in this review, so the sound-track route starts from two installs.

A coach's or stranger's clip forwarded by a parent is third-party content; its transcript reaches the parent's private agent the same way a forwarded PDF does and should be labelled as untrusted text.
safety: Option 2 keeps the audio on the Mac and sends only a transcript, like voice memos. No new vendor is added. Video from unknown senders never arrives because of the sender allowlist, and the document privacy gate still runs on the extracted text.
unverified: Whether gpt-6-sol accepts video input at all through the custom provider ids.
Whether a CLI media entry can hand back still frames as well as text; the docs show text output only.
Whether ffmpeg is installed for the happy user.
Whether gpt-6-sol could accept video input if the provider entry declared it; today the family's provider entries declare text and image only.

sources.title: Media understanding: bundled provider order
sources.supports: The bundled providers for video understanding are Google, Qwen and Moonshot; OpenAI is listed for images only.

review_notes: All five doc lines hold, but 'experimental' is the wrong label: watching a clip has no path on this provider set (blocked), and the sound-track route is ordinary build work that does not serve the entry's own example of a silent furnace panel. The honest deliverable today is a line telling the sender to send a photo.

name: iMessage tapbacks, typing bubble, polls and tap-to-approve (Private API mode)
description: What Happy's iMessage thread would gain if System Integrity Protection were turned off: a typing bubble and read receipts, a thumbs-up instead of a text reply, threaded replies, message effects, native polls, approving a request by tapback, and answering a multiple-choice question with a numbered reaction. All of it is unavailable in the current Basic mode.
example: Happy acknowledges 'add milk to the list' with a thumbs-up instead of a sentence, or asks the parents' group 'Pizza or tacos on Friday?' as a native poll.
how: channels.imessage in Private API mode: imsg injects a helper into Messages.app, which needs SIP disabled and library validation relaxed on the Mac mini; after that channels.imessage.actions.* and reactionNotifications apply. In Basic mode the plugin hides react, edit, unsend, reply, sendWithEffect and the group actions, and sends no typing or read signals.
depends_on: SIP disabled on the Gateway Mac (the roadmap keeps SIP on)
caveats: This is blocked by a deliberate rule rather than a defect: with SIP on, the channel is text and media send and receive only.
The docs warn that disabling SIP is a system-wide security trade-off and, on Apple Silicon, also stops iOS apps from being installed and run on that Mac.
The injected helper can drop out after a Messages restart or a macOS update and has to be relaunched.

name: Web egress guardrails for fetch and browser (LAN, SSRF, blocklists)
description: Makes sure nothing Happy fetches or browses can reach the home network (Hue bridge, printer, router page) or carry a secret along, and records which protections are hard limits and which are best effort. Every other web feature in this lens sits on top of it.
example: Trigger: an injected page tells the research agent to open the router's admin page; the call is refused before a request is sent, and the nightly eval has a case for it.
how: Gateway config, applies to the research agent. Keep `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` unset (strict is the default). Add known paste and tracker hosts to `tools.web.fetch.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames` and `browser.ssrfPolicy.blockedHostnames`. Leave `tools.web.fetch.headers` empty, because the model picks the URL and any header goes wherever it points. Leave `tools.web.fetch.provider` unset and do not install a fetch-provider plugin, so a failed fetch is never retried through a third party. Set `browser.evaluateEnabled: false`. Second layer if the roadmap's egress proxy is built: `proxy.proxyUrl` for the gateway's own HTTP clients. Add two eval cases to the M3 exit test: a LAN address, and a public URL that redirects to one. Added in review: the current config already has `browser.enabled: false` and `browser.allowSystemProfileImport: false` from M0 (cookie import from a real browser profile is otherwise on by default, and the agent tool has an action for it). Keep the first until WEB-02 ships and the second for good. Add `gateway.nodes.browser.mode: "off"` and, when the browser is switched on, `browser.defaultProfile: "openclaw"`. These guards were listed only under WEB-05, a record that will not be built, so they belong here. Leave the private-network key truly unset; do not write `false` (see caveats).
caveats: web_fetch blocks private hosts and re-checks redirects. The browser's check is weaker: the docs say its request interception is not a network firewall and can miss redirect hops, a popup's first request and Service Worker traffic.

The managed browser does not inherit the gateway's proxy environment, and strict SSRF mode blocks an explicit browser proxy flag unless private-network access is switched on. Putting the browser behind the roadmap's filtering proxy is therefore an open design conflict to settle before M3.
OpenClaw does not ship or run a proxy; `proxy.proxyUrl` only routes its own HTTP and WebSocket clients through one you operate.
There is no public-web allowlist setting: `allowedHostnames` only re-opens individual private hosts and `blockedHostnames` only denies. A per-agent site allowlist has to be a hook (WEB-03).

For web_fetch there is no public-web allowlist: its `allowedHostnames` only re-opens named private hosts and `blockedHostnames` only denies. The browser is different. In the installed source, an explicitly written `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: false` is not the same as leaving the key unset: hostname navigation is then refused unless the host matches `browser.ssrfPolicy.allowedHostnames`, while public IP-literal addresses still pass. That is a gateway-wide navigation allowlist in OpenClaw's own code: a useful second layer if the only browser on the gateway is a single-site one, unusable next to an open research browser, and a trap if someone writes `false` to be explicit (the research browser would stop loading hostnames). A per-agent site allowlist still has to be a hook (WEB-03).

The SSRF policy covers the `web_fetch` tool and the browser tool only. Host-side helpers that take a URL (the summarize wrapper in WEB-11, the print plugin's own download in F080, a feed watcher) run outside it and need their own scheme, host and resolved-address checks, or an injected URL reaches LAN devices through them.

Once research has web_fetch, the egress proxy cannot double as an exfiltration allowlist. Proxy routing is process-level, so one policy serves model calls, MCP traffic and research's fetches; a domain allowlist tight enough for the first two blocks the third. With research live, the proxy can deny private ranges and named hosts and nothing more. This is an inference from the routing description and it changes what the roadmap's Smokescreen allowlist can promise.

A hostname block list is not an exfiltration control: any host that is not on it works. Do not spend upkeep time curating paste and tracker lists. What counts is the private-network block, no headers, no fallback provider, and no private data in the agent that browses.
safety: Takes the home LAN out of reach of any agent that reads untrusted pages. It does not stop an injected page from making the agent request some public URL; that is contained by the research agent holding no private data and no accounts.
unverified: The roadmap's plan to drop LAN access inside the Colima VM would not cover a browser that runs on the host; this follows from where the process runs and was not tested.
Which hosts belong on the blocklist is a judgment call, not something the docs prescribe.
The explicit-false behaviour of the browser policy was read in the installed source only; the docs do not describe it and it was not exercised.
